None. EMPs do damage by amplifying the electrical charge passing through an object, like a massive power spike or surge. Additionally, EMPs are not magic force fields that destroy all electronics in a given radius, you can protect your equipment against EMPs relatively easily, the military does with most of their equipment. EMPs must be able to reach open contacts of the device to damage it, so insulating your device will protect it from an EMP. The easiest way to do this is to keep them inside. If an EMP goes off outside of your house, and your computer is in an interior room of the building with no windows and the doors are closed, your device will more than likely be fine. Your surge protector will be fucked cause the EMP will have surged the circuitry of your house (if you don't have a surge protector your PSU will be fried) but the rest of the computer should be fine.

For mobile devices or if you would like to have a window or even be outside with your computer, you will need to take it a step further by shielding and insulating your devices. Devices are designed with openings in them to allow for airflow for cooling. EMPs hijack these openings to access the contacts of your device and turn it into a paperweight. Military devices get around this by applying thick amounts of shielding to protect the device from EMPs (as well as jamming and shrapnel). This shielding has a side benefit of absorbing and holding heat, and since heat always spreads away from its source, the thick shielding allows you to run the device for a long while before it overheats due to no airflow. For example, if you place a cold cast-iron pan on a stove and put your hand in the pan, it will take quite a while for the pan to heat up and burn you because the thick metal has to absorb all that heat first before it will start radiating, especially compared to a thin pan, which will heat up very quickly. The issue is once that thick metal get hot, it stays hot, so the device will be inoperable for a considerable time before it cools down again. The military gets around this by having external heat sinks and fans to cool the metal shielding instead of directly cooling the electronics.

Our bodies are conductive only because of the saline water-salt mixture that is present in our body to cool us down. Fat is also an insulator because it's again mostly carbon. And most of our fat is concentrated in a layer between our skin and the rest of our body, creating an insulating layer against electricity. Another place of concentrated fat is in our brains. Nerve cells are coated in a layer of fat to protect them from stray signals from nearby neurons. There's a disease where lack of fat on the neurons causes paralysis, seizures, and eventually death, because the signals in your brain can't flow properly, essentially shorting itself out. So our body is designed to naturally resist external electrical signals.
